title: Osteology of the Lower Limb and Arches of the Foot
introduction: The skeleton of the lower limb comprises the femur, tibia, fibula, and bones of the foot (tarsals, metatarsals, and phalanges)[cite: 158]. While standing, body weight is transmitted sequentially from the vertebral column bilaterally to the hip bones, hip joints, femurs, knee joints, tibias, ankle joints, and bones of the foot[cite: 158].
learningOutcomes: 4.1 Describe the proximal end, shaft attachments, distal condyles, blood supply, and common fracture sites of the femur[cite: 158].
4.2 Identify the articulations, bony landmarks, neurovascular relations, and blood supply of the tibia[cite: 158].
4.3 Outline the anatomical features, tibiofibular joints, and fracture mechanisms of the fibula[cite: 158].
4.4 Classify the bones and anatomical regions of the foot (tarsals, metatarsals, and phalanges)[cite: 158].
4.5 Explain the bony composition, supports, and functions of the arches of the foot along with common clinical deformities[cite: 158].

content.heading: The Femur: Structure, Attachments, and Clinical Significance
content.body: The femur is the longest, heaviest, and strongest bone in the body, transmitting body weight from the hip bone to the tibia during standing[cite: 158]. Its proximal end consists of the head (which articulates with the acetabulum to form the hip joint), the neck, and the greater and lesser trochanters[cite: 158]. The cylindrical shaft is smoothly rounded anteriorly and laterally to give origin to knee extensors (vastus intermedius, articularis genu, vastus lateralis, and vastus medialis), while posteriorly the rough linea aspera provides attachment for thigh adductors (adductor brevis, adductor longus, adductor magnus) and the short head of biceps femoris[cite: 158]. The gluteal tuberosity receives deep fibers of gluteus maximus, the ischial part of adductor magnus inserts onto the adductor tubercle, and the spiral line continues anteriorly into the intertrochanteric line[cite: 158]. Distally, the medial and lateral condyles merge anteriorly as the patellar surface and are separated posteriorly by the intercondylar fossa, while the linea aspera splits into medial and lateral supracondylar lines enclosing the popliteal surface[cite: 158]. The femoral head and neck receive blood from the medial and lateral femoral circumflex arteries[cite: 158]. Clinically, the femoral neck is the narrowest and weakest part of the bone and is the most frequently fractured site (such as transcervical and intertrochanteric fractures)[cite: 158].

content.heading: The Tibia (Shin Bone)
content.body: The tibia is the second largest bone in the body and bears the majority of the leg's weight load (chiefly through its medial aspect), expanding at both ends to participate in five articulations: the knee joint, superior, middle, and inferior tibiofibular joints, and the ankle joint[cite: 158]. Its broad upper end features medial and lateral condyles, the intercondylar area superiorly, and the tibial tuberosity anteriorly[cite: 158]. The medial condyle has an oval superior articular surface and a posterior groove for semimembranosus, while the lateral condyle has a circular superior surface, a posterior inferolateral facet for the fibular head, and an anterior Gerdy's tubercle for the iliotibial tract[cite: 158]. The shaft has three borders—a sharp subcutaneous anterior border (shin), a medial border, and a lateral (interosseous) border attaching the interosseous membrane—and three surfaces (lateral, medial, and posterior)[cite: 158]. The narrower lower end projects medially as the subcutaneous medial malleolus (grooved posteriorly by tibialis posterior, giving apex attachment to the deltoid ligament, and bearing a lateral comma-shaped facet for the talus) and presents a lateral fibular notch for the inferior tibiofibular syndesmosis[cite: 158]. Anteriorly at the ankle, structures cross from medial to lateral as tibialis anterior, extensor hallucis longus, anterior tibial artery, deep peroneal nerve, extensor digitorum longus, and peroneus tertius; posteriorly they pass as tibialis posterior, flexor digitorum longus, posterior tibial artery, tibial nerve, and flexor hallucis longus[cite: 158]. Blood supply comes primarily from a nutrient artery and periosteal vessels derived from the anterior tibial artery[cite: 158].

content.heading: The Fibula (Calf Bone)
content.body: The fibula lies lateral to the tibia and is the thinnest, most slender long bone in proportion to its length[cite: 158]. Its small upper extremity sits behind the head of the tibia below the knee joint and is excluded from the knee joint itself; the head provides an anterior tubercle for peroneus longus and a posterior tubercle for the posterior ligament of the head and upper fibers of soleus[cite: 158]. Its lower extremity inclines forward and projects below the tibia to form the lateral malleolus of the ankle joint[cite: 158]. The fibula connects to the tibia via the superior tibiofibular (arthrodial) joint, the interosseous membrane syndesmosis, and the inferior tibiofibular syndesmosis[cite: 158]. Clinically, the lateral malleolus is prone to fracture through two main mechanisms: forced external rotation of the ankle drives the talus against the fibula causing a spiral fracture, whereas outward twisting (eversion) presses the talus against the lateral malleolus causing a transverse fracture[cite: 158].

content.heading: Bones of the Foot
content.body: The foot forms the distal part of the lower limb and contains 7 tarsal bones, 5 metatarsal bones, and 14 phalanges[cite: 158]. Anatomically, it is divided into three regions: the hindfoot (talus and calcaneus), the midfoot (navicular, cuboid, cuneiforms, and metatarsals), and the forefoot (phalanges)[cite: 158]. The 7 tarsal bones—talus, calcaneus, navicular, medial cuneiform, intermediate cuneiform, lateral cuneiform, and cuboid—sit between the distal leg bones and the metatarsals and participate with the tibia and fibula in the ankle joint[cite: 158]. The 5 metatarsals are miniature long bones numbered from medial to lateral, each having a proximal base, shaft, and distal head[cite: 158]. The 14 phalanges form the toes: digits 2 through 5 each contain proximal, middle, and distal phalanges, whereas the great toe has only proximal and distal phalanges[cite: 158].

content.heading: Arches of the Foot
content.body: Formed by the tarsal and metatarsal bones and reinforced by ligaments and tendons, the arches of the foot act as shock absorbers and springboards during walking, running, and jumping, and do not develop until about 2 to 3 years of age[cite: 158]. They are divided into longitudinal (medial and lateral) and transverse arches with plantar concavity[cite: 158]. The medial longitudinal arch is higher and comprises the calcaneus, talus, navicular, three cuneiforms, and first three metatarsals; it is supported by tibialis anterior, tibialis posterior, fibularis longus, plantar ligaments (including short plantar and plantar calcaneonavicular ligaments), and the medial ankle ligament[cite: 158]. The lateral longitudinal arch is much flatter and comprises the calcaneus, cuboid, and 4th and 5th metatarsals, supported by fibularis longus, flexor digitorum, intrinsic foot muscles, and the long plantar and plantar calcaneocuboid ligaments[cite: 158]. The transverse arch lies in the coronal plane, formed by the cuboid, cuneiforms, and metatarsal bases; its anterior transverse arch (formed by the metatarsal heads) is a complete arch because the 1st and 5th metatarsal heads touch the ground during standing[cite: 158].

content.heading: Clinical Correlates of the Foot
content.body: Pes cavus (high arch) is an unusually high medial longitudinal arch that causes foot pain radiating up to the ankle, leg, thigh, and hip[cite: 158]. Pes planus (flat foot) represents loss of the longitudinal arches from tendon trauma or congenital failure to develop, leading to foot and ankle pain in children and aching after prolonged activity in adults[cite: 158]. Clubfoot (talipes) is a congenital deformity in which shorter tendons twist the foot out of position, involving talus deformity and subluxation of the talocalcaneonavicular joint[cite: 158]. Hallux valgus is lateral deviation of the big toe at the metatarsophalangeal joint caused by wearing pointed high-heeled shoes, making the 1st metatarsal head prominent and creating a protective medial adventitious bursa (bunion)[cite: 158]. Hammer toe is a curling deformity caused by bending at the proximal interphalangeal (middle) joint, usually affecting the 2nd and 3rd toes[cite: 158].

inTextQuestions.question: Why is the neck of the femur the most frequently fractured part of the bone?
inTextQuestions.answer: Because it is the narrowest and weakest part of the femur[cite: 158].

inTextQuestions.question: Which structure attaches to Gerdy's tubercle on the anterior surface of the lateral tibial condyle?
Does the fibula participate in forming the knee joint?
inTextQuestions.answer: No, the upper extremity of the fibula sits below the knee joint and is excluded from its formation[cite: 158].

inTextQuestions.question: At what age do the arches of the foot typically develop?
inTextQuestions.answer: They do not develop until about 2 to 3 years of age[cite: 158].

saqs.question: Trace the pathway of body weight transmission through the lower limb in the standing position, and state the arterial supply to the femoral head and neck.
saqs.answer: Weight is transmitted from the vertebral column bilaterally to the hip bones, hip joints, femurs, knee joints, tibias, ankle joints, and finally the bones of the feet[cite: 158]. The femoral head and neck are supplied by the medial femoral circumflex artery and the lateral femoral circumflex artery[cite: 158].

saqs.question: List the structures crossing the posterior aspect of the lower end of the tibia from medial to lateral.
saqs.answer: From medial to lateral: tibialis posterior, flexor digitorum longus, posterior tibial artery, tibial nerve, and flexor hallucis longus[cite: 158].

saqs.question: Compare the two main mechanisms that produce fractures of the lateral malleolus of the fibula and the fracture pattern each creates.
saqs.answer: Forced external rotation of the ankle pushes the talus against the fibula, causing a spiral fracture of the lateral malleolus; outward twisting (eversion) of the foot presses the talus against the lateral malleolus, causing a transverse fracture[cite: 158].

saqs.question: Compare the bony composition and ligamentous supports of the medial and lateral longitudinal arches of the foot.
saqs.answer: The medial longitudinal arch consists of the calcaneus, talus, navicular, three cuneiforms, and first three metatarsals, supported by plantar ligaments (including short plantar and plantar calcaneonavicular ligaments) and the medial ankle ligament[cite: 158]. The flatter lateral longitudinal arch consists of the calcaneus, cuboid, and 4th and 5th metatarsals, supported by the long plantar and plantar calcaneocuboid ligaments[cite: 158].

saqs.question: Differentiate between pes cavus, pes planus, hallux valgus, and hammer toe.
saqs.answer: Pes cavus is an unusually high medial longitudinal arch causing radiating lower limb pain[cite: 158]; pes planus (flat foot) is loss of the longitudinal arches causing aching after activity[cite: 158]; hallux valgus is lateral deviation of the big toe at the metatarsophalangeal joint associated with a medial bunion[cite: 158]; and hammer toe is a curling deformity at the proximal interphalangeal joint usually affecting the 2nd and 3rd toes[cite: 158].
